claim: Recent studies have provided evidence for the concurrent encoding of sensory percepts and visual working memory (VWM) contents across visual areas.
source: Recent studies have provided evidence for the concurrent encoding of sensory percepts and visual working memory (VWM) contents across visual areas
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in the field.

claim: The VWM code in several visual regions did not fully generalize between different time points, suggesting a dynamic code.
source: First, we found that the VWM code in several visual regions did not fully generalize between different time points, suggesting a dynamic code.
evidence: This claim is based on temporal cross-decoding analysis results presented in the study.

claim: The lack of generalization of VWM code across time points was due to shifts in coding spaces across time.
source: A more detailed analysis revealed that this was due to shifts in coding spaces across time.
evidence: This claim is based on neural subspace analysis results presented in the study.

claim: VWM and feature-matching sensory distractors are encoded in coding spaces that do not fully overlap.
source: We find that VWM and feature-matching sensory distractors are encoded in coding spaces that do not fully overlap
evidence: This claim is based on neural subspace alignment analysis presented in the study.

claim: The separation between VWM and distractor coding spaces decreases when distractors negatively impact behavioral performance in recalling the target.
source: but the separation decreases when distractors negatively impact behavioral performance in recalling the target.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of neural subspace alignment between experiments with different behavioral outcomes.

claim: Visual working memory (VWM) allows for a brief maintenance of visual stimuli that are no longer present within the environment.
source: Visual working memory (VWM) allows for a brief maintenance of visual stimuli that are no longer present within the environment (Curtis and D'Esposito, 2003; Goldman Rakic, 1995; D'Esposito and Postle, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The contents of VWM are present throughout multiple visual areas, starting from V1.
source: Previous studies have revealed that the contents of VWM are present throughout multiple visual areas, starting from V1 (Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Harrison and Tong, 2009; Christophel et al., 2012; Ester et al., 2015; Rademaker et al., 2019; Rademaker et al., 2019; Riggall and Postle, 2012; Serences et al., 2009; Christophel et al., 2017; Curtis and Sprague, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Both VWM contents and sensory percepts are multiplexed in occipital and parietal regions.
source: Recent studies that had participants remember a stimulus while simultaneously being presented with sensory stimuli during the delay period have found supporting evidence that both VWM contents and sensory percepts are multiplexed in occipital and parietal regions (Rademaker et al., 2019; Iamshchinina et al., 2021a; Bettencourt and Xu, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Dynamic coding is the change of the population code encoding VWM representations across time.
source: One proposed mechanism to achieve the separation between sensory and memory representations is dynamic coding (Stokes et al., 2020; Stokes, 2015; Stroud et al., 2024): the change of the population code encoding VWM representations across time.
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Frontal regions display dynamic population coding across the delay during the maintenance of category and spatial contents in the absence of interference.
source: Frontal regions display dynamic population coding across the delay during the maintenance of category (Meyers et al., 2008) and spatial contents in the absence of interference (Murray et al., 2017; Spaak et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Frontal regions show dynamic recoding of the memoranda after sensory distraction.
source: and also show dynamic recoding of the memoranda after sensory distraction (Parthasarathy et al., 2017; Parthasarathy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The visual cortex in humans displays dynamic coding of contents during high load trials.
source: The visual cortex in humans displays dynamic coding of contents during high load trials (Sreenivasan et al., 2014b)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The visual cortex in humans displays dynamic coding during a spatial VWM task.
source: and during a spatial VWM task (Li and Curtis, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The sensory bottom-up visual pathway primarily projects to the cytoarchitectonic Layer 4 in V1.
source: For example, evidence from neuroanatomy indicates that the sensory bottom-up visual pathway primarily projects to the cytoarchitectonic Layer 4 in V1
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to neuroanatomical evidence.

claim: Feedback projections culminate in superficial and deep layers of the cortex.
source: while feedback projections culminate in superficial and deep layers of the cortex (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to neuroanatomical evidence.

claim: VWM signals preferentially activate the superficial and deep layers in humans.
source: Functional results are in line with neuroanatomy by showing that VWM signals preferentially activate the superficial and deep layers in humans (Lawrence et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to functional neuroimaging research.

claim: VWM signals preferentially activate the superficial and deep layers in nonhuman primates.
source: and nonhuman primates (van Kerkoerle et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to nonhuman primate research.

claim: Perceptual signals are more prevalent in the middle layers.
source: while perceptual signals are more prevalent in the middle layers (Lawrence et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to functional neuroimaging research.

claim: Memory and sensory representations are orthogonally coded in the auditory cortex.
source: regional multiplexing of multiple items could potentially rely on rotated representations, as seen in memory and sensory representations orthogonally coded in the auditory cortex (Libby and Buschman, 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A sequence of multiple spatial locations is stored in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) using rotated representations.
source: and in the storage of a sequence of multiple spatial locations in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Xie et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Nonoverlapping orthogonal representations segregate attended and unattended VWM representations in both humans and trained recurrent neural networks.
source: Nonoverlapping orthogonal representations have also been seen in both humans and trained recurrent neural networks as a way of segregating attended and unattended VWM representations (Wan et al., 2022; Wan et al., 2023; van Loon et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants memorized a sensory stimulus while simultaneously being presented with sensory distractors.
source: In the first experiment, the delay period was either left blank (no-distractor) or a noise or randomly oriented grating distractor was presented (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental design from the reanalyzed dataset.

claim: Decoding accuracies were above chance in all three conditions from as early as 4 s after the onset of the delay period.
source: In all three conditions and throughout all regions of interest (ROIs), we found clusters where decoding was above chance (Figure 1c–e, black outline; nonparametric cluster permutation test against null; all clusters p<0.05) from as early as 4 s after the onset of the delay period.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical testing of decoding results shown in figures.

claim: Decoding on the diagonal was highest during no-distractor compared to noise and orientation distractor trials in most ROIs.
source: We found that decoding on the diagonal was highest during no-distractor compared to noise and orientation distractor trials in most ROIs (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of decoding accuracies across conditions shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Dynamic coding clusters were found in all three conditions.
source: Despite a high degree of temporal generalization, we found dynamic coding clusters in all three conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of temporal cross-decoding matrices.

claim: Some degree of dynamic coding was observed in all ROIs but LO2 in the noise distractor and no-distractor trials.
source: Some degree of dynamic coding was observed in all ROIs but LO2 in the noise distractor and no-distractor trials
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of dynamic coding elements across ROIs.

claim: Dynamic coding was only present in V1, V2, V3, V4, and IPS in the orientation distractor condition.
source: while it was only present in V1, V2, V3, V4, and IPS in the orientation distractor condition (Figure 1c–e, blue outline).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of dynamic coding elements shown in figures.

claim: Most dynamic elements occurred between the encoding and early delay periods (4–8 s), and the late delay and retrieval (14.4–16.8 s).
source: Across all conditions, most dynamic elements occurred between the encoding and early delay periods (4–8 s), and the late delay and retrieval (14.4–16.8 s).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the dynamicism index across time.

claim: During the noise distractor trials in V1, dynamic coding occurred during the middle of the delay period.
source: Interestingly, during the noise distractor trials in V1, we also saw dynamic coding during the middle of the delay period; the multivariate code not only changed during the onset and offset of the noise stimulus, but also during its presentation and throughout the extent of the delay.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the dynamicism index in V1 during noise distractor trials.

claim: The decoding accuracies across all conditions were nominally lower in the second experiment compared to the first.
source: The decoding accuracies across all conditions, including the no-distractor condition, were nominally lower in the second experiment compared to the first.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of decoding results between experiments.

claim: In some ROIs in Experiment 2, the information about the target was not present during the delay period.
source: In some ROIs, the information about the target was not present during the delay period (chance decoding on the diagonal; Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–d).
evidence: This claim is based on decoding results shown in supplementary figures.

claim: SNR differences are unlikely to give rise to dynamic coding clusters.
source: These simulations indicate that SNR differences are unlikely to give rise to dynamic coding clusters.
evidence: This claim is based on simulation results testing the effect of SNR on dynamic coding.

claim: All three conditions showed significant above-baseline principal angles (aPAs).
source: All three conditions showed significant aPAs (Figure 2d; cyan stars; permutation test; p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical testing of principal angles shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The early (4.8 s) and late (16.8 s) delay subspaces showed the highest number of significant pairwise aPAs in all conditions.
source: Corresponding to the results from the cross-decoding analysis, the early (4.8 s) and late (16.8 s) delay subspaces showed the highest number of significant pairwise aPAs in all conditions
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of pairwise principal angles across time points.

claim: Noise distractor trials had all pairwise aPAs, including the early and late subspaces, being significant.
source: with noise distractor trials having all pairwise aPAs, including the early and late subspaces, being significant.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of pairwise principal angles in noise distractor trials.

claim: Stable coding of the distractor was found in all ROIs with only a few dynamic elements in V2 and V3.
source: We found stable coding of the distractor in all ROIs with only a few dynamic elements in V2 and V3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on temporal cross-decoding analysis of the distractor shown in supplementary figures.

claim: When cross-decoded, the sensory distractor and target orientation had lower decoding accuracies in the early visual cortex compared to when trained and tested on the same label type.
source: When cross-decoded, the sensory distractor (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) and target orientation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b) had lower decoding accuracies in the early visual cortex compared to when trained and tested on the same label type, indicative of a non-generalizing code.
evidence: This claim is based on cross-decoding analysis between target and distractor shown in supplementary figures.

claim: A significant above-baseline principal angle was found between the target and distractor subspaces in Experiment 1.
source: We quantified the difference between the target and distractor subspaces and found a significant aPA between them (p=0.0297, one-tailed nonparametric permutation test; Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical testing of principal angles shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The above-baseline principal angle between target and distractor subspaces was significant in Experiment 2 (p<0.001).
source: The aPA was significant (p<0.001, one-tailed nonparametric permutation test; Figure 3d), but nominally smaller than in the first experiment.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical testing of principal angles shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The above-baseline principal angle was nominally smaller in Experiment 2 than in Experiment 1.
source: The aPA was significant (p<0.001, one-tailed nonparametric permutation test; Figure 3d), but nominally smaller than in the first experiment.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of principal angles between experiments.

claim: Decoding accuracy was higher in the no-distractor trials compared to both orientation and noise distractor trials across all ROIs, but IPS.
source: Decoding accuracy was higher in the no-distractor trials compared to both orientation and noise distractor trials across all ROIs, but IPS (Figure 4a, red and blue lines, p<0.05, cluster permutation test) across several stages of the delay period.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical comparison of decoding accuracies shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The cross-decoding accuracies from no-distractor to distractor trials were significantly lower than the no-distractor in all ROIs but V4 (in both noise and orientation) and LO2 (only noise).
source: We found that the cross-decoding accuracies were significantly lower than the no-distractor in all ROIs but V4 (in both noise and orientation) and LO2 (only noise).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical comparison of cross-decoding accuracies.

claim: Information was recovered in areas V2 and V3AB in the noise distractor condition when the decoder was trained and tested on the same distractor condition.
source: We found that indeed information was recovered in areas V2 and V3AB in the noise distractor condition (Figure 4b, pairwise permutation test).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical comparison of decoding accuracies shown in Figure 4b.

claim: A temporal cross-decoding analysis where all training time points were no-distractor trials had less dynamic coding in early visual regions when compared to the temporal cross-decoding matrix when trained and tested on noise distractor trials.
source: Additionally, a temporal cross-decoding analysis where all training time points were no-distractor trials had less dynamic coding in early visual regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) when compared to the temporal cross-decoding matrix when trained and tested on noise distractor trials (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of dynamic coding patterns between different training conditions shown in figures.

claim: The first experiment did not yield a behavioral deficit in the feature-matching orientation distractor trials.
source: In this study, the first experiment did not yield a behavioral deficit in the feature-matching orientation distractor trials
evidence: This claim refers to behavioral results from the original study (Rademaker et al., 2019).

claim: The second experiment impacted target recall in the feature-matching flickering orientation trials.
source: while the second experiment impacted target recall in the feature-matching flickering orientation trials (Rademaker et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim refers to behavioral results from the original study (Rademaker et al., 2019).

claim: Feature-matching distractors behaviorally bias retrieved VWM contents.
source: There is evidence from behavioral and neural studies that show interactions between perception and VWM: feature-matching distractors behaviorally bias retrieved VWM contents (Rademaker et al., 2015; Mallett et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: VWM representations influence perception.
source: VWM representations influence perception (Teng and Kravitz, 2019; Kang et al., 2011; Gayet et al., 2013; Gayet et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neural visual VWM representations in the early visual cortices are biased toward distractors.
source: neural visual VWM representations in the early visual cortices are biased toward distractors (Lorenc et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The fidelity of VWM neural representations within the visual cortex negatively correlates with behavioral errors when recalling VWM during a sensory distraction task.
source: and the fidelity of VWM neural representations within the visual cortex negatively correlates with behavioral errors when recalling VWM during a sensory distraction task (Hallenbeck et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There was no significant difference in the coding format of VWM between orientation distractor and no-distractor trials.
source: To our surprise, we did not observe a significant difference in the coding format of VWM between orientation distractor and no-distractor trials.
evidence: This claim is based on cross-decoding analysis between conditions.

claim: The sensory distractor stimulus occupies a distinct coding space throughout its presentation during the delay, while the coding space of the target remains the same in both orientation and no-distractor trials.
source: We suggest that the sensory distractor stimulus occupies a distinct coding space throughout its presentation during the delay, while the coding space of the target remains the same in both orientation and no-distractor trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results based on the observed patterns.

claim: Layer-specific coding differences in perception and VWM might explain the findings.
source: Layer-specific coding differences in perception and VWM might explain these findings (Lawrence et al., 2018; Lawrence et al., 2019; Iamshchinina et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The sensory distractor neural subspace might predominantly reside in the bottom-up middle layers of early visual cortices.
source: Specifically, the sensory distractor neural subspace might predominantly reside in the bottom-up middle layers of early visual cortices
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on prior knowledge of cortical layer organization.

claim: The neural subspace encoding VWM might primarily occupy the superficial and deep layers.
source: while the neural subspace encoding VWM might primarily occupy the superficial and deep layers.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on prior knowledge of cortical layer organization.

claim: Dynamic coding and temporally stable coding spaces play a role in helping multiplex perception and VWM within visual areas.
source: Together, these results indicate a role of dynamic coding and temporally stable coding spaces in helping multiplex perception and VWM within visual areas.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Different coding spaces within the same region might be a more general mechanism of segregating feature-matching stimuli.
source: Considering previous findings, we posit that different coding spaces within the same region might be a more general mechanism of segregating feature-matching stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization based on the study's findings and prior research.

claim: Six participants completed Experiment 1.
source: In Experiment 1, six participants performed two tasks while in the scanner: a VWM task and a perceptual localizer task.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design from the reanalyzed dataset.

claim: Seven participants completed Experiment 2.
source: In Experiment 2, seven participants performed the same type of VWM task with three trial types: no-distractor, flickering orientation distractor, and a naturalistic (gazebo or face) distractor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design from the reanalyzed dataset.

claim: The target orientation grating was presented centrally for 500 ms in Experiment 1.
source: Following the cue, the target orientation grating was presented centrally for 500 ms, followed by a 13 s delay period.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design from the reanalyzed dataset.

claim: The delay period was 13 s in Experiment 1.
source: Following the cue, the target orientation grating was presented centrally for 500 ms, followed by a 13 s delay period.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design from the reanalyzed dataset.

claim: In trials with the distractor in Experiment 1, a stimulus was presented centrally for 11 s in the middle of the delay period.
source: In the trials with the distractor, a stimulus of the same shape and size as the target grating was presented centrally for 11 s in the middle of the delay period (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design from the reanalyzed dataset.

claim: The orientation and noise distractors reversed contrast at 4 Hz in Experiment 1.
source: The orientation and noise distractors reversed contrast at 4 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design from the reanalyzed dataset.

claim: Participants completed 27 runs of the task in Experiment 1, resulting in a total of 108 trials per condition.
source: Across three sessions, participants completed 27 runs of the task, resulting in a total of 108 trials per condition.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design from the reanalyzed dataset.

claim: In Experiment 2, the distractors alternated between being displayed on and off at 4 Hz.
source: However, unlike Experiment 1, where distractors exhibited contrast reversals, the distractors in Experiment 2 alternated between being displayed on and off at 4 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design from the reanalyzed dataset.

claim: The data were acquired using a simultaneous multi-slice EPI sequence with a TR of 800 ms.
source: The data were acquired using a simultaneous multi-slice EPI sequence with a TR of 800 ms, TE of 35 ms, flip angle of 52°, and isotropic voxels of 2 mm.
evidence: This is a description of the MRI acquisition parameters from the reanalyzed dataset.

claim: Voxels were selected that reliably responded to both the donut-shaped orientation perception task and the no-distractor VWM task.
source: In contrast to the original study, we reduced the size of our ROIs by selecting voxels that reliably responded to both the donut-shaped orientation perception task and the no-distractor VWM task.
evidence: This describes the voxel selection procedure used in the current analysis.

claim: Periodic support vector regression (pSVR) was used to predict the target orientation from the multivariate BOLD activity.
source: We used pSVR to predict the target orientation from the multivariate BOLD activity (Weber et al., 2024).
evidence: This describes the decoding method used in the analysis.

claim: PSVR uses a regression approach to estimate the sine and cosine components of a given orientation independently.
source: PSVR uses a regression approach to estimate the sine and cosine components of a given orientation independently and therefore accounts for the circular nature of stimuli.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of pSVR.

claim: A cluster-based approach was used to test for significance for above-chance decoding clusters.
source: We used a cluster-based approach to test for significance for above-chance decoding clusters (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007)
evidence: This describes the statistical testing approach used in the analysis.

claim: Dynamic coding clusters were defined as elements where the multivariate code at a given time point did not fully generalize to another time point.
source: Dynamic coding clusters were defined as elements within the temporal cross-decoding matrix, where the multivariate code at a given time point did not fully generalize to another time point; in other words, an off-diagonal element was significantly smaller in accuracy compared to its two corresponding on-diagonal elements (aij < aii and aij < ajj, Figure 1b).
evidence: This defines the operational definition of dynamic coding used in the analysis.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to the high-dimensional activity patterns at each time point to identify the two axes that explained maximal variance across orientations.
source: Specifically, we followed a previous methodological framework (Li and Curtis, 2023) and applied a principal component analysis (PCA) to the high-dimensional activity patterns at each time point to identify the two axes that explained maximal variance across orientations (see Figure 2 and Methods).
evidence: This describes the neural subspace analysis method used in the study.

claim: The above-baseline principal angle (aPA) measures the alignment between the 2D subspaces encoding the VWM representations.
source: The aPA measures the alignment between the 2D subspaces encoding the VWM representations: the higher the angle, the smaller the alignment between two subspaces and an indication of a changed neural coding space.
evidence: This defines the aPA metric used in the analysis.
